posts.title: Better than on admission, worse than before
posts.insight: Measuring recovery from the day of admission hides loss of function that happened before the person arrived. In one large cohort, about 1 in 3 older medical inpatients went home less able than two weeks before admission, mostly because of loss before arrival that was not regained.
posts.angle: Progress measured from the worst day looks like recovery; the useful reference point is the person two weeks before the illness. Position (judgement): record the pre-illness level and state the gap at discharge.
posts.position_basis: mixed: cohort findings on decline (empirical); the recording habit is clinical judgement

captions.x:
A ward note saying "improving since admission" can be true while the person goes home less able than before they fell ill.

In a US study of 2,293 people aged 70 and over on medical wards, 35 in 100 left hospital less able to wash, dress, eat, transfer or use the toilet than two weeks before admission.

23 in 100 had lost that ability before they arrived and had not regained it. 12 in 100 lost it during the stay.

The data are over 20 years old, but a 2019 review found about 3 in 10 older people still lose independence in daily activities after an acute stay.

We should record the level two weeks before the illness, and say at discharge how far the person is from it.
captions.linkedin:
A ward note saying "improving since admission" can be true while the person goes home less able than before they became ill.

The reference point decides what you see. Measured from the day of admission, most people improve, because admission is often their worst day. Measured from two weeks before the illness, a different picture appears.

In a US cohort of 2,293 people aged 70 and over admitted to medical wards (Covinsky 2003), 35 in 100 went home less able in basic daily activities (washing, dressing, eating, transfers, toileting) than they had been two weeks before admission.

Most of that loss came before the ward. 23 in 100 had declined before arrival and not recovered by discharge. 12 in 100 declined during the stay. Another 20 in 100 declined before admission and got the ability back.

The gap widened with age: 23 in 100 at 70 to 74, 63 in 100 at 90 and over (crude figures).

Limits: function was reported by patients or relatives, the five activities do not include walking, and the data are more than 20 years old. A 2019 review pooling 7,375 older adults found about 3 in 10 lost independence after an acute stay, with little change over time, though methods varied.

A second study found hospital records usually did not say whether the person could manage individual daily tasks before admission.

My view: we should record what the person could do two weeks before the illness, and write at discharge how far they are from that level. "Two weeks before: dressed alone. Now: needs help with buttons" tells the next team far more than "improving".

In a US study of 2,293 medical inpatients aged 70+ (data over 20 years old), 35 in 100 went home less able to wash, dress or use the toilet than two weeks before admission. Most had lost it before arrival.

Record the pre-illness level, not only progress since admission.

posts.title: Still doing it, but differently
posts.insight: A yes or no question about difficulty misses people who have changed how or how often they do a task. That change (preclinical disability) marks people who are already slower and weaker and more likely to develop difficulty.
posts.angle: Revised angle: add one history question about changed method or frequency; state population limits; do not claim acting early prevents disability.
posts.position_basis: mixed: cohort findings (empirical); adding the question to the history is clinical judgement

captions.x:
"Any difficulty with stairs?" "No." That answer can miss the person who now takes them one at a time, holding the rail with both hands.

In a Baltimore study of more able women aged 70 to 80 (1990s), those who had changed how or how often they walked or climbed stairs, without difficulty, were already slower and weaker. Over the next 18 months they were more likely to develop difficulty. A Finnish study found the same in men and women.

The studies were of more able women recruited in the 1990s, plus one smaller Finnish group.

Add one question: "Have you changed how you do this, or how often, because of your health?"
captions.linkedin:
"Any difficulty with stairs?" "No."

That answer can miss the person who now takes the stairs one at a time, holding the rail with both hands. Researchers call this stage preclinical disability: the task still gets done, but the method or frequency has changed.

In a Baltimore study of 436 women aged 70 to 80 (Fried 2001), women who had changed how or how often they walked half a mile or climbed 10 steps, but reported no difficulty, were measured as slower, weaker and less steady than women with no change. They were not as affected as women who reported difficulty.

Over the next 18 months, women who had changed how they walked or climbed stairs had about 3 to 4 times the odds of developing difficulty, even after allowing for walking speed (Fried 2000). A later analysis found new changes predicted new walking difficulty a year and a half on, with wide uncertainty (Weiss 2012). A Finnish study of people aged 75 to 81 found the same pattern in men and women (Mänty 2007).

Limits: the main studies were of women aged 70 to 79 in Baltimore, the more able two thirds of their age group, recruited in the mid-1990s. The researchers proposed this stage as a point to offer help; these studies did not test whether acting then prevents disability.

The question used in the research: "Have you changed the way you walk half a mile, or how often you do this, because of a health or physical condition?"

I think it belongs in a functional history, next to the difficulty question.
captions.bluesky:
"Any difficulty with stairs?" misses people who now climb them differently.

In more able women aged 70 to 80 in Baltimore (1990s), changing method without difficulty went with slower walking and later difficulty. A smaller Finnish study agreed.

Ask: "Have you changed how or how often you do this?"

posts.title: Frailty can move both ways
posts.insight: Frailty often changes over time. About 14 in 100 older people living at home became less frail over about 4 years, while 29 in 100 became more frail; improvement was most often by one step.
posts.angle: Public reassurance without false hope: show worsening next to improvement, show that improvement is mostly one step, and give the guideline first step (strength exercise; protein or calories if losing weight).
posts.position_basis: mixed: pooled cohort findings and guideline recommendations (empirical); the advice to ask for reassessment is judgement

captions.x:
Being told you are frail describes where you are now. It can change.

In 16 studies of 42,775 older people living at home, followed for about 4 years, 14 in 100 became less frail, 29 in 100 became more frail, and 57 in 100 stayed the same (one definition of frailty).

Most improvement was one step. Of people who were frail, 40 in 100 moved to the milder early stage (prefrail); only 3 in 100 lost all signs of frailty.

International guidelines put exercise that includes strength training first, with extra protein or calories if you are losing weight or undernourished.

Ask for your frailty to be reassessed after a few months of that.
captions.linkedin:
Being told you are frail describes where you are now. It can change, in both directions.

A 2019 review pooled 16 studies of 42,775 older people living at home, followed for about 4 years on average (Kojima 2019). Of those reassessed:

1. About 14 in 100 became less frail.
2. About 29 in 100 became more frail.
3. About 57 in 100 stayed the same.

So worsening was about twice as common as improvement. Improvement was real, though, and getting back to no signs of frailty was far more common from the early stage. Among people in the early stage (prefrail, meaning they met one or two of five frailty signs such as slow walking or weak grip), about 23 in 100 later met none.

Among people who were frail, most improvement was one step. About 40 in 100 moved to the prefrail stage, and only about 3 in 100 later met none of the criteria. A US study of 754 people found the same: moving straight from frail to not frail at all was very rare.

These figures use one definition of frailty and people living at home.

What helps? International frailty guidelines recommend, as the first step, an exercise programme that includes strength training. They recommend protein or calorie supplements for people who are losing weight or undernourished, and a fuller assessment for anyone found to be frail (Dent 2019).

If you have been told you are frail, you can ask two things: what exercise to build strength is available to you, and when your frailty will be looked at again.
captions.bluesky:
Frailty can change. Over about 4 years, 14 in 100 older people at home became less frail and 29 in 100 more frail.

Most improvement was one step, to a milder stage.

Guidelines put strength exercise first. If you've been called frail, ask when it will be reassessed.

posts.title: Two routes to the same CFS 6
posts.insight: The Clinical Frailty Scale counts dependence from any cause, so the same score can describe moderate dementia or a physical disability. The number alone does not say which.
posts.angle: Write the reason next to the number (practice suggestion, marked as judgement). No claim that outcomes differ by route.
posts.position_basis: mixed: scale definitions and developer guidance (empirical/documentary); recording habit is clinical judgement

captions.x:
Two people can both score 6 on the Clinical Frailty Scale for different reasons.

The scale counts dependence from any cause. Its developers say level 6 can describe someone with moderate dementia who washes and dresses only with prompting, or someone whose thinking is fine but who needs a person standing by because of physical disability.

The guidance also says that in dementia the frailty level generally follows the stage of dementia.

The score is a clinical judgement and the start of a care plan. I would write the reason next to it: "CFS 6 (moderate dementia; walks independently)".
captions.linkedin:
Two people can both score 6 on the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) for different reasons.

The scale describes how much help a person needs, whatever the cause. Level 7, for example, means complete dependence for personal care, whether the cause is physical or cognitive.

Level 6 describes someone who needs help with all activities outside the home and with housework, often has trouble with stairs, needs help to bathe, and may need prompting or someone standing by while dressing.

The developers point out that this pattern fits two quite different people: someone with moderate dementia who can wash and dress only with prompting, and someone whose thinking is fine but whose physical disability means they need a person standing by (Rockwood and Theou 2020).

The guidance adds that in dementia the frailty level generally follows the stage of dementia: mild dementia with level 5, moderate with 6, severe with 7. "Generally" means it guides scoring; it is not a fixed rule.

The developers describe the score as a clinical judgement that summarises function, cognition and mobility, and as the start of a care plan, not a substitute for one. Predicting outcome also needs the severity of the current illness.

My suggestion, which is judgement and has not been tested in an outcome study: write the reason next to the number. "CFS 6 (moderate dementia; walks independently)" and "CFS 6 (heart failure; needs standby help to wash)", to take an invented example, send the next reader in different directions.

I have not found studies comparing outcomes by the route to a score, so I would not claim one route does better after surgery or rehabilitation.
captions.bluesky:
A Clinical Frailty Scale score of 6 can mean moderate dementia with prompting to dress, or intact thinking with a physical disability. The scale counts dependence from any cause.

Write the reason next to the number.

posts.title: What the frailty number in a letter means
posts.insight: "CFS" in a letter means the Clinical Frailty Scale, from 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill). Levels 5 to 8 describe increasing need for help; level 4 needs no daily help. It is meant to describe your usual self.
posts.angle: A plain translation of the scale plus questions the person can ask.
posts.position_basis: empirical (scale definitions and developer guidance); the suggestion to ask is judgement

captions.x:
Seen "CFS 6" in a hospital letter? It means the Clinical Frailty Scale, which runs from 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill).

Levels 1 to 3 are fit or managing well. Level 4 is very mild frailty: you are slowed down, but need no help from others day to day.

Levels 5 to 8 describe increasing need for help. At 5, help with things like money, transport or heavy housework. At 6, help outside the home, with housework and bathing. At 7 and 8, help with all personal care.

The score should describe your usual self, such as two weeks before this illness. You can ask what it was based on.
captions.linkedin:
Seen "CFS 6" in a hospital letter with no explanation? It means the Clinical Frailty Scale.

The scale has 9 levels, from 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill). In plain words:

1. Levels 1 to 3: very fit, fit, or managing well.
2. Level 4, very mild frailty: symptoms slow you down, but you do not need help from others day to day.
3. Level 5, mild frailty: help with things like money, transport and heavy housework.
4. Level 6, moderate frailty: help with everything outside the home, with housework and with bathing.
5. Level 7, severe frailty: needing others for all personal care.
6. Level 8, very severe frailty: the same, and approaching the end of life.
7. Level 9: expected to live less than about 6 months, but not otherwise severely frail. Many are still active.

So levels 5 to 8 describe increasing need for help. Older letters may use earlier names, such as "vulnerable" for level 4.

The score is meant to describe how you usually are, not how you seem while ill. The developers give the example of how someone was two weeks before coming into hospital. Level 9 is the one exception, based on the current illness.

Doctors use the score to help judge how someone may cope with illness and treatment and to plan care. It is one input, and it depends on a clinician's judgement (Rockwood and Theou 2020).

You can ask: what was my score based on, does it describe me before this illness, and what is it being used for?
captions.bluesky:
"CFS 6" in a letter means the Clinical Frailty Scale, 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill). Levels 5 to 8 mean increasing need for help; level 4 needs no daily help.

It should describe your usual self. Ask what it was based on.

posts.title: An occupational therapist, a nurse and a handyperson
posts.insight: A US trial that worked on both the person and the home reduced difficulty with washing and dressing at 5 months, but the gain faded by 12 months and a later trial after hospital did not repeat it.
posts.angle: Revised angle: good care that looks at both person and house, with the limits stated as plainly as the benefit; action as a question, no provider named.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial findings (empirical); the suggestion to ask for a combined look is judgement

captions.x:
Difficulty at home comes from two places: what your body can do, and what your home asks of it.

A US trial of 300 older people on low incomes sent an occupational therapist, a nurse and a handyperson to about half of them, working on goals each person chose. At 5 months they reported less difficulty with washing, dressing and the toilet than people who had social visits. 8 in 10 who answered said it made life easier a great deal, against 4 in 10.

Household tasks did not clearly improve, the difference faded by 12 months, and a 2025 trial after hospital did not repeat it.

If tasks are getting harder, ask whether someone can look at both you and your home.
captions.linkedin:
Difficulty at home comes from two places: what your body can do, and what your home asks of it.

A US trial called CAPABLE worked on both (Szanton 2019). 300 older people on low incomes in Baltimore, who had difficulty with everyday tasks, took part. About half were offered up to 10 home visits over 5 months: up to 6 from an occupational therapist, up to 4 from a nurse, and repairs or equipment from a handyperson. The visits worked on goals each person chose. The comparison group had 10 friendly social visits.

After 5 months, people who had the programme reported less difficulty with basic tasks such as washing, dressing, using the toilet and getting in and out of bed. Their average difficulty scores were about 30% lower than the comparison group's (a relative comparison of scores, not of people).

About 8 in 10 said it made their life easier a great deal, against about 4 in 10 with social visits.

The limits deserve equal space:

1. Household tasks such as shopping and cooking did not clearly improve.
2. Seven months after the visits stopped, the difference had faded.
3. A 2025 trial of the same programme in 268 people just home from hospital did not clearly improve basic daily tasks, though walking and stairs improved more.
4. Most participants were Black women with low incomes in one US city.

What I take from it: an assessment of difficulty at home should look at the person and the house together. If daily tasks are getting harder for you, ask whether an occupational therapist can look at how you do things and at your home.
captions.bluesky:
A US trial of 300 older people on low incomes sent an occupational therapist, nurse and handyperson to half. At 5 months they had less difficulty washing and dressing than those given social visits, but it faded by 12 months.

Ask for someone to look at you and your home together.

posts.title: Where comprehensive geriatric assessment has shown benefit
posts.insight: Hospital comprehensive geriatric assessment has high-certainty evidence: about 3 more in 100 alive and at home, 3 to 4 fewer in care homes. For frail people at home the evidence is much weaker.
posts.angle: The same name covers different services; judge a service by the plan and follow-up, and match claims to the evidence for the setting.
posts.position_basis: mixed: Cochrane findings (empirical); the standard for services is judgement

captions.x:
Comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) has good evidence in hospital and much weaker evidence at home.

In a Cochrane review of 29 hospital trials, about 60 in 100 were alive and at home 3 to 12 months later with CGA, against 56 in 100 without (16 trials reported this). About 15 in 100 were in a care home, against 19. Deaths: 23 in 100 in both.

For frail people living at home, 21 studies showed probably little or no difference in deaths or care home moves; fewer unplanned admissions is possible, on weak evidence.

In these reviews CGA means a team assessment followed by a coordinated plan that is followed up. A service using the name should be able to show both.
captions.linkedin:
Comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) has good evidence in hospital and much weaker evidence for frail people living at home. The name covers both, so it helps to know which is which.

In the Cochrane reviews, CGA means a team assessing a frail older person's medical, mental and functional problems, then making and following up a coordinated plan of treatment. A form or a one-off assessment on its own is not what was tested.

Hospital (Ellis 2017; 29 trials, 13,766 people; each result below comes from 14 to 21 of these trials):

1. Alive and living at home 3 to 12 months later: about 60 in 100 with CGA, 56 in 100 without (high certainty).
2. In a care home: about 15 in 100 against 19 in 100.
3. Deaths: 23 in 100 in both groups.
4. Help needed with daily tasks: little or no difference.

The effects are modest, and trials were mostly in high-income countries over several decades. An earlier analysis suggested dedicated wards did better than visiting teams; the 2017 update said the data were too few to tell.

Frail people at home (Briggs 2022; 21 studies): probably little or no difference in deaths, and little or no difference in care home moves over about a year. It may reduce unplanned hospital admissions, but that evidence is low certainty.

My judgement: a service that uses the name should be able to show the plan and the follow-up, not only the assessment. Claims for community services should match the more modest evidence, without dismissing them.
captions.bluesky:
Hospital geriatric assessment: about 60 in 100 alive and at home at 3 to 12 months vs 56 without; fewer in care homes; same deaths.

For frail people at home, evidence is weaker.

The tested model ends in a followed-up plan, not a form.

posts.title: Which frailty?
posts.insight: Applied to the same 5,377 people, 35 frailty tools labelled between about 1 in 100 and 2 in 3 as frail, and often disagreed about who. Results from one tool do not transfer automatically to people labelled by another.
posts.angle: Fallback for C05-14. Lead with the same-sample finding; the first question about any 'frail' study is which tool and cut-off.
posts.position_basis: mixed: cohort analysis (empirical); the 'first question' is judgement following from it

captions.x:
Which tool decided who was frail? Ask that before applying any study "in frail older people".

Researchers applied 35 published frailty tools to the same 5,377 people aged 60 and over in England. Depending only on the tool and cut-off, the share called frail ranged from about 1 in 100 to about 2 in 3.

The tools often disagreed about which individuals were frail: for almost 9 in 10 pairs, agreement was moderate at best (kappa 0.10 to 0.83 overall).

The authors concluded most tools can't be swapped for one another.
captions.linkedin:
Which tool decided who was frail? I would ask that before applying any study "in frail older people" to the person in front of me.

Aguayo and colleagues (2017) applied 35 published frailty scores to the same 5,377 people aged 60 and over in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. Because the people were the same, differences came from the tools alone.

The share classed as frail ranged from about 1 in 100 to about 2 in 3, depending on which tool and cut-off was used.

The tools also disagreed about which individuals were frail. Agreement between pairs ranged from kappa 0.10 (little better than chance) to 0.83 (strong), and almost 9 in 10 pairs showed moderate agreement at best. In the authors' worked illustration, at an assumed prevalence of 20%, the worst pairs would label about 3 in 10 people differently.

One caveat: the scores were built from the study's own variables, so some approximate the original tools.

Between studies the spread is also wide. Community studies have reported frailty in anywhere from 4 in 100 to 59 in 100 older people, partly because of definitions and partly because of who was studied. Pooled estimates from studies of people aged 50 and over put physical definitions at about 1 in 8 and tools counting many health problems at about 1 in 4.

The authors concluded that most scores can't be treated as interchangeable. My practical reading: a trial result, a guideline threshold or a service criterion based on one tool applies most directly to people identified the same way.
